name: DIM (diindolylmethane)

card.summary: A broccoli-derived compound sold as an estrogen-metabolism supplement; the appearance and hormone claims are mostly untested in humans.
card.note: Registered human trials concern cancer and other conditions, not appearance or physique.

quick.overview:
DIM is a compound the body forms when it digests indole-3-carbinol, which is found in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli and cabbage. It is sold as a dietary supplement, and in bodybuilding and hormone-optimisation circles it is promoted as a way to influence how estrogen is metabolised.

Laboratory research has examined its possible biological effects, mostly in cancer models. No published trial has tested DIM for appearance, muscle or body-composition outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say DIM shifts estrogen breakdown toward metabolites they regard as favourable. In laboratory work it has been reported to inhibit histone deacetylase enzymes and to bind weakly to cannabinoid receptors [1]. Whether these effects occur at supplement intakes in people, or change appearance, has not been established by the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: DIM is sold as a dietary supplement in the US rather than as an approved drug. Safety data in healthy users are limited to small early-phase trial registrations. A homeopathic menopause product listing DIM as one ingredient carries a label advising people who are pregnant or breast-feeding to ask a health professional first [2].

lead: 3,3'-Diindolylmethane (DIM) is a compound formed in the body from indole-3-carbinol, which occurs in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, Brussels sprouts, cabbage and kale. It is sold as a dietary supplement [1].

In bodybuilding and hormone-focused communities, DIM is marketed and discussed as an estrogen-metabolism supplement, often alongside other products in this category. Laboratory research has examined its biological effects, particularly in cancer models, and Wikipedia notes that it has been studied as a histone deacetylase inhibitor in vitro [1].
No published trial has tested DIM for appearance-related outcomes. Clinical trial registrations list small early-phase studies in cancer, lupus, thyroid disease and healthy volunteers [3][4][5][6].
infobox: Formed from indole-3-carbinol in cruciferous vegetables [1]
Sold as a dietary supplement in the US

paras: DIM has the chemical formula C17H14N2 and a molar mass of about 246 g/mol [1]. It is not eaten directly in meaningful amounts; it arises when stomach acid converts indole-3-carbinol from cruciferous vegetables [1]. Supplements deliver DIM itself, in some products in specially formulated forms.

In vitro work reported that DIM acts as an inhibitor of histone deacetylases 1, 2 and 3, and that it binds weakly to the cannabinoid receptors CB1 and CB2 [1]. A 2023 laboratory study reported that DIM reduced biofilms of Streptococcus mutans, a bacterium involved in dental plaque; as of 2025, Wikipedia notes that no clinical trial had confirmed an effect on plaque in people [1].
No studies found that test DIM for appearance, muscle, body composition or hormone outcomes in healthy men or women.

Registered clinical trials of DIM concern other conditions. These include a phase 1 study in BRCA1 mutation carriers [3], a phase 1 study in men with prostate cancer that had not responded to hormone therapy [4], a phase 1 study in healthy volunteers [5], studies in breast cancer [6][7], and early studies in lupus and proliferative thyroid disease, two of which were terminated [8][9]. The registrations list design and enrolment, and the results are not summarised here.

A US-listed homeopathic menopause product names DIM among many ingredients; its label states that its claims are based on homeopathic principles and have not been reviewed by the FDA [2]. In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities, DIM is typically discussed in the context of estrogen management; no community sources were available to quote directly for this article.
